newsitem.title: CROATIA: UN dismisses chances of Croatian Serb 'referendum'.
newsitem.headline: UN dismisses chances of Croatian Serb 'referendum'.

text.p: The United Nations said on Tuesday Serbs in Croatia's last breakaway enclave were unlikely to stage a referendum on their electoral status despite their vow to do so, and its results would not be binding anyway.

Serbs in Eastern Slavonia are upset at Croatian plans to split the U.N.-administered Danube River region into two counties that will be reintegrated with the rest of Croatia after communal elections on April 13.

Serb leaders fear the division will deny them any local electoral majorities but Croatian and U.N. officials note the region was never a single district before 1991, when Serb rebels seized it and drove out Croat neighbours.
The Serbs' enclave council decided late last week to hold a referendum on April 6 as to whether Eastern Slavonia should remain territorially united after reintegration.
"We do not expect this referendum to take place," said Doug Coffman, a spokesman for the U.N. Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), based in its main town Vukovar.
He noted that the Serbs' demand for a single district had already been rejected as untenable by the Croatian government and by a U.N. Security Council statement on the enclave's future.
"We expect responsible Serb leadership (in Eastern Slavonia) to follow a wiser course of action," Coffman said.

"The Serbs make up a vast majority of the area's population now but such a referendum cannot be binding because it will not represent the future population," he said, alluding to the pending return of the region's former Croat majority.

"Serbs should do more responsible things to prepare for reintegration like organising political parties, choosing candidates and registering to vote, which they're already doing (to some extent)," he told Reuters by telephone from Vukovar.

Croatian state officials and media assailed the referendum plan as a stalling manoeuvre by die-hard Serb nationalists to divert attention from Zagreb's guarantees of wide-ranging minority rights for the Serb population.
Western diplomats say the Serbs stand to gain electoral majorities in up to 10 of some 30 municipalities but only if they turn out to vote in significant numbers.

UNTAES expects up to 20 percent of the 120,000-odd Serbs will flee to nearby Serbia rather than accept restoration of Croatian authority, due to be completed by early summer. Serb leaders anticipate 50 percent or more will go.
Coffman said several thousand Serbs had moved personal goods across the Danube River border to Serbia since January 1 but added, "No mass exodus is going on by any means".

It was hard to tell whether Serbs were leaving for good or "just diversifying their assets" while waiting to see whether Croatia upholds its pledges of minority protection, said another U.N. official.
UNTAES is examining a revised Croatian government list of 175 wanted Serb war criminals, a fraction of the previously mentioned number, presumed living in the enclave.
UNTAES has pressed the Croatian government for months to issue a precise, reliable list to help persuade Serbs not to flee en masse for fear of random arrest after reintegration.
